(p-2944) Surah al-Anfal

It is Medinan, or, except for the verse "And [remember] when those who disbelieve plot against you" [al-Anfal: 30] and the seven verses following it, in which case it is Meccan. Its verses number seventy-five.

It is named "al-Anfal" (the spoils of war) because it opens with them (the subject of this surah), and because they are the final point of what is mentioned in it regarding the matter of warfare.

(p-2945) In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful

Discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[1] "They ask you about the spoils. Say, 'The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah, set right what is between you, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers.'"

"They ask you about the spoils. Say, 'The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah, set right what is between you, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers.'"

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that Surah al-Anfal was revealed concerning Badr.

Imam Ahmad narrated from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I witnessed Badr with him. The people met, and Allah, the Exalted, defeated the enemy. One group set off in their pursuit, defeating and killing them; another group turned to the camp, collecting and gathering it; and another group surrounded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that the enemy could not catch him unawares. When night came and the people returned to one another, those who had gathered the spoils said: 'We collected and gathered them, so no one has any share in them.'

Those who had gone out in pursuit of the enemy said: 'You have no more right to them than we do; we drove the enemy away from them and defeated them.'

Those who had surrounded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'You have no more right to them than we do; we encircled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), fearing that the enemy might catch him unawares, and we were occupied with him.' Then the verse was revealed: 'They ask you about the spoils...' and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided them equally among the Muslims."

(p-2946) This hadith was also narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, and by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and al-Hakim authenticated it.

The wording of Ibn Ishaq from 'Ubadah is: "It was revealed concerning us, the companions of Badr, when we disputed about the nafl (extra portion) and our characters deteriorated because of it. Allah took it from our hands and placed it in the hands of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who divided it among the Muslims equally."

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "On the day of Badr, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever does such-and-such will have such-and-such as nafl.' The young men of the people hastened to do so, while the elders remained under the banners.

When the spoils were gathered, they came seeking what had been promised to them. The elders said: 'Do not take precedence over us, for we were a reserve for you; had you been routed, you would have returned to us.' They disputed, and Allah, the Exalted, revealed: 'They ask you about the spoils...'" This indicates that the disputes were varied, and that the verse was revealed to settle them.

Al-Anfal means the spoils of war, plural of nafal (with a fatha on the na and a sukun on the fa, as in nafl), which means booty; that is, every gain that the Muslims obtained from the property of the people of war.

Ibn Taymiyyah said: it is so called because it is an addition to the wealth of the Muslims; that is, nafl is applied to an addition, as in al-Taj, and from it comes nafilah, for voluntary prayer, because it is an addition to the obligatory prayer.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: "Say, 'The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger'": al-Mahayimi said: That is, they are not in exchange for the jihad; its equivalent is the reward in the Hereafter, and these spoils are over and above that. They have left the possession of the polytheists and become pure property of Allah and His Messenger. The Messenger is the khalifah who gives them, according to what Allah shows him, to whomever he wills, since he (ﷺ) was given absolute authority over them; so he divided them among them equally, and gave to whoever asked him for a gift.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "On the day of Badr my brother 'Umayr was killed, and I killed Sa'id ibn al-'As and took his sword, which was called Dhu al-Kutayfah. I brought it to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Go and throw it into the spoils heap.' I returned with what only Allah knows of grief over my brother's killing and the loss of my spoils.

I had not gone far when Surah al-Anfal was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Go and take your spoil.'"

Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih, narrated from Sa'd ibn Malik, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Allah has healed me today from the polytheists, so give me this sword.' He said: 'This sword belongs neither to you nor to me; place it down.'

So I placed it down and returned, saying to myself: 'Perhaps this sword will be given today to someone who does not endure trials as I did.' Then a man was calling me from behind. I said: 'Has Allah revealed something concerning me?' He said: 'You had asked me for the sword, but it does not belong to me; it has been given to me, so it is yours.' And Allah revealed this verse: 'They ask you about the spoils...'"

Notes:

First: Some scholars held that the spoils of Badr were divided without the one-fifth (khums) being set aside, and that afterwards the verse of the khums was revealed, abrogating the first ruling (naskh; abrogation).

Ibn Kathir said: "There is scrutiny in this." The hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning the two she-camels he obtained from the khums on the day of Badr refutes it. The correct view is that the verse is mujmal (general) and muhkam (firm), and the verse of the khums explained its channels of expenditure.

Second: It is narrated from 'Ata' that he interpreted al-anfal as whatever came over from the polytheists to the Muslims without fighting, such as a beast, a slave-woman, or goods. He said: "It is a nafl for the Prophet (ﷺ), who does with it as he wills."

Ibn Kathir said: "This implies that he interpreted al-anfal as fay', which is what is taken from the disbelievers without fighting."

I say: That the word nafl applies to it is beyond doubt, but that it is specifically what is meant by the verse is not supported by the occasion of its revelation mentioned above, especially His saying: "and set right what is between you", which points to the dispute that preceded.

Ibn Kathir then said: Ibn Jarir preferred that it means the extra portion given above the division, i.e., what is given to the warrior over and above his share of the booty, and what I said earlier applies here too.

Al-Razi related from al-Qadi that all these meanings are possible for the verse. He said: There is no evidence in it to prefer one of them over another; and if the traditions confirm something that indicates a specific meaning, it is adopted, otherwise all are possible.

Just as each of them is permissible, so too is intending all of them together permissible, for there is no contradiction between them, since the word nafl applies to each.

Third: It occurred to al-Zamakhshari that the Muslims disputed over the spoils of Badr: to whom does the ruling over them belong, to the Muhajirun or to the Ansar, or to both of them together? So they were answered that the one who decides about them is the Messenger, and no one else has any ruling over them.

Abu al-Su'ud followed al-Zamakhshari in his presentation of what was mentioned, and added to it his reliance on him, in a tedious lengthy manner. I do not know from where this narration reached them.

For the narrators of reports did not record it in their Sahih collections or their Sunan, nor did the biographers such as Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Hisham. Is it possible for the Muslims to dispute over the ruling on the spoils and contend over their authority while the Messenger was among them? When was such a thing known from their conduct? Glory be to You, this is a great slander! But it is opinion, may Allah fight it! It casts aside the books of Sunnah and pure taqlid (blind imitation), whose adherent does not concern himself with the realities of things, nor desire to know them or examine them by reason; he places his foot upon the foot, where he is compliant to the opinions of others, submissive to them, confirming whatever his mouth utters, whether it be worthless or valuable. O Allah, illuminate our insight with Your grace.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: "So fear Allah": that is, regarding disputing and quarrelling, and be united and brotherly for the sake of Allah.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: "and set right what is between you": that is, the states between you, meaning the conditions that exist among you, until they become states of harmony, love and agreement.

(p-2949) As for His, the Exalted, saying: "and obey Allah and His Messenger": that is, in His division among you, according to what Allah, the Exalted, shows him.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: "if you are believers": it is connected to the three commands.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made taqwa, setting right what is between people, and obedience to Allah and His Messenger, among the requirements and necessities of faith, to inform them that the perfection of faith depends on fulfilling these. So the meaning of His saying "if you are believers" is: if you are of perfect faith.

Then the Exalted explained who is meant by the "believers" by mentioning their noble qualities, which entail the three qualities mentioned, as an encouragement for them to carry out the commands mentioned. So He, glory be to Him, said:

The discussion of the exegesis of His saying, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿Indeed, the believers are those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely.﴾

﴿Indeed, the believers﴾ — that is, the perfect ones, the sincere in it (al-Mukhlisun fihi) — ﴿are those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾ — that is, His right (haqquhu) or His threat (wa'iduhu) — ﴿their hearts tremble﴾ — that is, they are startled at His remembrance, and their skin shivers out of apprehension lest they have not fulfilled His right, and out of awe of His majesty, the might of His dominion, His seizing of the disobedient, and His punishment.

Al-Jushami said: If it is asked why the description of them with trembling is appropriate here, while in His saying: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28], then our answer to this has several aspects:

Among them: their hearts find rest upon remembering His blessings, and tremble out of fear of His punishment for committing His acts of disobedience.

Among them: their hearts find rest upon knowing His oneness, His promise, and His threat; then at that they tremble before His commands and prohibitions, out of fear of falling short in the obligatory duties and of advancing into acts of disobedience, and the future state changes. End of quotation.

﴿And when His verses are recited to them﴾ — that is, His proofs, which is the Qur'an — ﴿they increase them in faith﴾ — that is, in certainty and tranquility of soul, added to what they already have; for the convergence of proofs is stronger for what they indicate, and more firm for its footing.

(p-2950) Al-Bukhari and others among the imams have cited this verse and its like as evidence for the increase of faith and its variation in hearts, as is the position of the majority of the Ummah. Indeed, more than one scholar has related a consensus upon it, such as al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Abu 'Ubayd.

﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾ — that is, they hope for none other than Him, fear none other than Him, and do not entrust their affairs to anyone else.

Since He, exalted is He, mentioned among their good deeds the deeds of the heart — fear, sincerity, and reliance — He followed them with the deeds of the limbs, such as prayer and charity, by His saying, glory be to Him:

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted, saying:

[3] ﴿Those who establish prayer and from what We have provided them they spend.﴾

﴿Those who establish prayer﴾ i.e., the obligatory prayer with its limits and its pillars, at its appointed times.

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is a qualifier (na't) of the first relative pronoun, or an elucidation (bayan) of it, or it is in the accusative by way of praise (nasb 'ala al-madh).

His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ is general, covering zakah and all kinds of righteousness and acts of nearness to Allah (qurubat).

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 8, verse 4:

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[4] ﴿Those are the true believers. For them are ranks with their Lord, and forgiveness and a generous provision.﴾

﴿Those are the true believers﴾ meaning: there is no doubt about their faith.

As for ﴿true﴾ (ḥaqqan): it is either an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning "a true faith," or an emphatic verbal noun for the sentence, meaning "that is truly so," as in your saying, "He is truly the servant of Allah."

ʿAmrah ibn Murrah said (regarding this verse): "The Qur'an was only revealed in the language of the Arabs, like your saying: 'So-and-so is truly a master (sayyid),' though there are masters (sādah) among the people; and 'So-and-so is truly a merchant (tājir),' though there are merchants (tujjār) among the people; and 'So-and-so is truly a poet (shāʿir),' though there are poets (shuʿarāʾ) among the people." End of quotation.

It seems he intended to refute the one who claimed that ﴿ḥaqqan﴾ belongs with what follows, ﴿for them are ranks﴾, as an emphasis for it, and that the sentence is complete at ﴿the believers﴾. This claim is to be safeguarded against, given the wise style of the revelation.

Some exegetes have here taken an extreme position on a well-known question: may one say, "I am a believer truly"?

Al-Tusi said in (Naqd al-Muhassal): The Mu'tazilah and those who followed them say: certainty does not admit doubt or cessation. So the saying of one who says, "I am a believer, if Allah wills," is not valid except in the case of doubt or fear of cessation. And what suggests either of these may not be said for the sake of blessing. End of quotation.

Al-Ghazali, in the Ihya', expanded on this question and answered those who permitted it with several answers:

Among them: fear regarding the final outcome, since faith is contingent upon a good end.

Among them: guarding against self-praise.

Among them: other matters; see it at length.

Ibn Hazm said in (al-Fasl): Our view on this question is that this is a quality a person knows about himself. If he knows that he affirms Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and Muhammad (ﷺ), and everything he brought, and that he professes all of that with his tongue, then it is obligatory for him to acknowledge it, as the Exalted commanded in His saying: ﴿And as for the favor of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [al-Duha: 11].

There is no blessing more emphatic, more excellent, or more deserving of thanks than the blessing of Islam. So it is obligatory for him to say: "I am a believer and a Muslim with certainty before Allah, the Exalted, at this time of mine."

There is no difference between his saying "I am a believer and a Muslim" and his saying "I am black or I am white," and likewise all his attributes about which there is no doubt. This is not a matter of self-praise or boasting in any way, because it has been made obligatory upon him to preserve his blood by the testimony of monotheism.

As for the saying of Ibn Mas'ud, "I am a believer, if Allah wills," it is sound in our view, because Islam and faith are names transferred from their original linguistic meanings to all righteousness and acts of obedience.

Ibn Mas'ud only prohibited definitive assertion in the sense that one has fulfilled all acts of obedience, and this is correct.

Whoever claims this for himself has undoubtedly lied. Nothing prevents a person from saying "I am a believer" in the sense of "I affirm (muṣaddiq)."

(p-2952) As for the saying of those who prohibit it, "Whoever says 'I am a believer' should say that he is among the people of Paradise," the answer is: we say that if we die in the state we are in now, then we will undoubtedly enter Paradise.

The proof of this is that it has been established from the texts of the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and the consensus that whoever believes in Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), and in everything he brought, and does not commit what is disbelief, will be in Paradise. However, we do not know what will be done to us in this world, and we do not feel safe from the plotting of Allah, the Exalted, nor from His misguiding, nor from the scheming of Satan; we do not know what we will earn tomorrow, and we seek refuge in Allah from abandonment. End of the words of Ibn Hazm, may Allah have mercy on him.

He excelled in what he conveyed.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For them are ranks with their Lord﴾, meaning: stations and lofty degrees in Paradise. ﴿And forgiveness﴾, meaning: overlooking of their misdeeds. ﴿And a generous provision﴾, which is what He has prepared for them of the bliss of Paradise.

Note:

Al-Jushami said: The verse indicates several things:

Among them: that faith is a legal term for three characteristics: speech, belief, and action, contrary to what the Murji'ah say, because fear and increase in assurance are acts of the heart, and reflection and contemplation are likewise, while prayer and spending are acts of the limbs, and reliance (tawakkul) involves acts of the heart and limbs.

Then he explained at its end that whoever combines these characteristics is the true believer.

Among them: that it indicates that faith increases and decreases, because these acts of obedience increase and decrease, and this is explicitly stated by His saying: ﴿When they are recited to them, it increases them in faith﴾ [al-Anfal: 2].

Among them: that the obligation upon reciting the Qur'an is reflection and contemplation on what He commanded and forbade, and promised and threatened, so that it leads to desire and fear, and that is an incitement to obedience and a deterrent from sins.

Among them: the obligation of reliance upon Him. Reliance is of two kinds: one in the worldly life and one in religion.

As for the worldly life, certain characteristics are necessary:

Among them: that one seeks the interests of his worldly life through the means that are available to him, and does not seek what is forbidden.

(p-2953) Among them: if lawful provision is withheld, he does not turn to what is forbidden.

Among them: that he does not show impatience at hardship, but follows the path of patience and believes that what he is in is a benefit to him.

Among them: that whatever blessings he is provided with after these come from Him, the Exalted, either directly or through an intermediary.

Among them: that he does not withhold his rights out of fear of poverty.

Among them: that he does not waste in spending nor become impoverished.

When these characteristics come together, he becomes one who relies upon Allah.

As for what some of them claim, that tawakkul means neglecting oneself and abandoning work, this is nothing.

Allah, the Exalted, has commanded spending and working, and it is established from the Companions, who are the masters of Islam, that they engaged in trade, agriculture, and labor; likewise the Successors, and by this Allah has established the custom.

The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the Bedouin to tie his camel and rely upon Allah.

As for reliance in religion, it has several characteristics:

Among them: that one performs the obligations and avoids the prohibitions, for by this he reaches Paradise and mercy.

Among them: that he asks Him for success and protection.

Among them: that he sees all his blessings as from Him, when they are obtained through His guidance, empowerment, and kindness.

Among them: that he does not trust in his obedience entirely, but obeys, avoids sins, hopes for the mercy of his Lord, and fears His punishment; at that point he is one who relies upon Allah.

Then al-Jushami said: The verse also indicates that one who abandons prayer and zakat is not a believer, contrary to the saying of the Murji'ah. End of quotation.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[5] ﴿Just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth, though a party of the believers were averse.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: The *kaf* in *kama* (كَما) is the *kaf al-tashbih* (the particle of comparison). Its governing element (al-'amil) may be understood in several ways. It may be the sense of the verb indicated by His saying ﴿Say: The spoils belong to God﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], with the implied meaning: "He removed the spoils from their hands in truth, just as He brought you forth in truth." Or it may be the sense of *al-haqq* (truth), meaning: "This mention is true, just as your bringing forth was true." Or it may be the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), the thing being compared, meaning: "Their condition in their aversion to the distribution of spoils to the raiders is like the condition of your being brought forth from your house for the battle, in their aversion to it" (as will come in the detailed account of the story).

This is the view of al-Farra' (d. 207 AH), for he said: The *kaf* makes this story, which is the bringing forth of the Prophet from his house, resemble the earlier story, which is their questioning about the spoils and their aversion to what happened in it, although the former is more appropriate to their condition.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from your house﴾ — by it is meant Medina, or Medina itself, because it was his abode; that is, his going forth toward Badr.

Some claimed that what is meant is the Prophet's ﷺ departure from Mecca to Medina for the Hijrah (emigration), but this is baseless, because it contradicts the context of the Badr narrative in the verses that follow.

The summary of the story is that Abu Sufyan came from al-Sham with a caravan of great merchandise. The Prophet ﷺ and his companions went out to seize it as spoils. Quraysh learned of this, so Abu Jahl and the fighters of Mecca went out to defend it, and they were the *nafir* (the mobilized force). Abu Sufyan took the caravan by the coastal route and escaped. It was said to Abu Jahl: "Turn back." But he refused and proceeded to Badr.

The Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions and said to them: "God has promised me one of the two groups." They agreed with him to fight the *nafir*, but some of them disliked that and said: "We were not prepared for it," as God, exalted is He, said:

(p-2955)

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[6] ﴿They argue with you concerning the truth after it has become clear, as though they were being driven toward death while they look on.﴾

﴿They argue with you concerning the truth﴾ — this being the fighting (jihad) and responding to the call to march out (al-nafir). ﴿After it has become clear﴾ — i.e., it had become evident to them that they would be given victory in it. ﴿As though they were being driven toward death while they look on﴾ — i.e., they disliked fighting with the dislike of one who is being driven toward death while looking at its causes. This was due to the smallness of their number and their lack of preparation.

For it is related that they were three hundred and nineteen men, among them two horsemen: al-Miqdad and al-Zubayr, though it is said that only the first was a horseman. The polytheists were a thousand, possessing both numbers and equipment. Within this there is an allusion that they were being led only toward victory and booty, by the true promise.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[7] ﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the unarmed one would be yours, while Allah intended to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the roots of the disbelievers.﴾

﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups﴾, the caravan or the army (al-nafir), ﴿that it would be yours﴾, ﴿and you wished﴾, i.e., you loved, ﴿that the unarmed one would be yours﴾, which is the caravan, not the one with the might (dhat al-shawkah), which is the army. Al-shawkah means weapons or their sharpness.

﴿And Allah intended to establish the truth﴾, i.e., to confirm it and make it prevail, and this is the call of His Messenger, ﴿by His words﴾ [Yunus: 82], i.e., by His revealed verses and His commands regarding this matter, ﴿and to cut off the roots of the disbelievers﴾, i.e., to uproot them so that none of them remains.

Then the Exalted explained the wisdom in choosing for them the one with might and granting them victory over it, by His saying:

The commentary on the words of Allah, Exalted is He:

[8] ﴿That He might establish truth and nullify falsehood, even if the criminals dislike it.﴾

﴿That He might establish truth and nullify falsehood﴾ means: that He might establish the true religion (al-din al-haqq) and efface the false religion (al-din al-batil) by uprooting its people, despite the strength of their might. ﴿Even if the criminals dislike it﴾ means: the polytheists (al-mushrikun) dislike that.

Then He, Exalted is He, reminded them of their seeking His aid (iltija') and their asking Him for victory (istimdad) on the Day of Badr, and of His reinforcing them at that time, through His saying, glorified is He:

The Explanation of His Words, may He be exalted:

[9] ﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another."﴾

﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾ means: you asked Him for ghawth (relief), which is deliverance from hardship, and aid through victory over them. ﴿And He answered you﴾ means: your supplication. ﴿I will reinforce you﴾ means: I will help you ﴿with a thousand of the angels, following one another﴾ — with kasr on the dal (mut'bi'in? no: mourdifin with a kasra), meaning: successive, some following upon others; or "those who follow" others (murdifin ghayrahum).

It is also read with fatha on the dal, on the meaning that God caused the Muslims to be followed by them (ardafa al-muslimin bihim), or "those who are followed by others" (murdafin bi-ghayrihim), i.e., by other angels.

It is also read (bi-ālāfin) in the plural, as will come.

Muslim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab told me: "When the day of Badr came, the Messenger of God ﷺ looked at the polytheists, who were a thousand, while his companions were three hundred and some ten men. So the Prophet of God ﷺ faced the qibla, then stretched out his hands, and began calling upon his Lord, saying: 'O God, fulfil for me what You promised me. O God, give me what You promised me. O God, if this band of the people of Islam perishes, You will not be worshipped on earth.' He continued calling upon his Lord, stretching out his hands, until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr came to him, took his cloak, placed it back on his shoulders, then embraced him from behind and said: 'O Prophet of God! Your urging of your Lord is enough, for He will surely fulfil for you what He promised you.' Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾."

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet ﷺ said on the day of Badr: "This is Jibril, holding the head of his horse, wearing the equipment of war."

Al-Bukhari narrated from Mu'adh ibn Rifa'a, from Rafi' al-Zuraqi, from his father — who was among those who witnessed Badr — who said: "Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'How do you count the people of Badr among you?' He said: 'Among the best of the Muslims' — or a similar phrase. He said: 'And likewise those of the angels who witnessed Badr.'"

Remarks:

First: Al-Jushami said: The verse indicates that an angel may take on the likeness of a human being without leaving his being an angel, by changing his extremities but not the parts by which they became living. What is denied is that anyone can have power to change forms; rather, we say that God is the One who has power over that.

End.

Second: Al-Zamakhshari said: And from al-Suddi: (with thousands of the angels) — in the plural — to agree with what is in Surat Al 'Imran.

If you say: How is one who reads in the singular to be excused, when he does not explain (murdifin) as the reinforcement of the angels by other angels, and (murdafin) as their being followed by others?

I say: The intended "thousand" is those among them who fought, or the leading ones among them, whom the others are followers of. End.

Shams al-Din Ibn al-Qayyim said in "Zad al-Ma'ad", in the section on the battle of Badr:

If it is said: Here He mentions that He reinforced them with a thousand, while in Surat Al 'Imran He says: ﴿When you said to the believers: "Will it not suffice you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 124] ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear God, and they come upon you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 125] How then is the reconciliation between them?

(p-2958) It is said: Scholars differed about this reinforcement of three thousand and that of five thousand, on two views:

One: That it was on the day of Uhud, and it was a reinforcement conditioned upon a condition; when the condition was not fulfilled, the reinforcement lapsed. This is the view of al-Dahhak and Muqatil, and one of the two narrations from 'Ikrima.

The second: That it was on the day of Badr. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, and the other narration from 'Ikrima, and a group of exegetes chose it.

The argument of these is that the context indicates this, for He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And God had already helped you at Badr, when you were humble. So fear God, that you may be grateful.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 123] ﴿When you said to the believers...﴾ [124] ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear God﴾ [125] up to His saying: ﴿And God did not make it except as good news for you, and that your hearts might be reassured thereby.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 126]

These said: When they sought help, He reinforced them with a thousand, then reinforced them with a full three thousand, then with a full five thousand, because they were patient and feared God. This gradual progression and succession of reinforcement was better in its effect, more strengthening to them, and more joyful for them than if it came once, and it is like the successive revelation and its descent time after time.

The first group said: The story is in the context of Uhud, and the mention of Badr was inserted as a parenthesis within it. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And when you set out from your family to station the believers at their posts for battle — and God is Hearing, Knowing﴾ [121] ﴿when two groups among you were about to lose heart, though God was their ally, and upon God let the believers rely﴾ [122], then said: ﴿And God had already helped you at Badr, when you were humble﴾ [123], so His mention of His favours upon them, in that He gave them victory at Badr while they were humble, then He returned to the story of Uhud and reported the words of His Messenger to them: ﴿Will it not suffice you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?﴾ [124], then He promised them that if they were patient and feared God He would reinforce them with five thousand.

So this is from the words of His Messenger, and the reinforcement at Badr is from the words of God, the Exalted; this one is with five thousand, and the reinforcement of Badr with a thousand; this one is conditioned upon a condition, and that one is unconditional.

The story in Surat Al 'Imran is the story of Uhud, complete and lengthy, and Badr is mentioned in it as a parenthesis.

(p-2959) The story in Surat al-Anfal is the story of Badr, complete and lengthy. So the context in Al 'Imran is other than the context in al-Anfal. What clarifies this is that His saying: ﴿and they come upon you suddenly, this﴾ [125] — Mujahid said: this is the day of Uhud. This requires that the reinforcement mentioned therein is not what it is; so his saying that the reinforcement with this number was on the day of Badr, and their coming upon them suddenly that day of Uhud, is not valid. And God knows best. End.

And His, may He be exalted, saying

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[10] ﴿And Allah made it not but as good news and so that your hearts would be assured thereby. And victory is not except from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise.﴾

﴿Allah made it﴾ means: this reinforcement. ﴿Not but as good news﴾ means: a glad tiding for you of victory. ﴿And so that your hearts would be assured thereby, and victory is not except from Allah﴾ means: without there being any partnership in it for anyone else. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise.﴾

Some of the wise (ḥukamāʾ) said: In this verse, Exalted is He mentioned the wisdom behind informing them of the victory, and that He intends by it their glad tidings, their tranquility, and their reliance upon Him. This is more conducive to the strength of resolve, for when the worker is certain that the One who subdues the universe is with him, that thought elevates him and makes him the strongest of people and the most capable of facing difficult affairs. This is unlike what is thought by the decadent, ignorant, lazy, and despairing people who have lost hope in the mercy of Allah, who made reliance (tawakkul) a pretext for idleness, and so they earned wrath upon wrath. End of quote.

Then, Glorified is He, reminded them of other blessings which He made a means of their victory and of His care for them, so He said:

The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

[11] ﴿When He covers you with drowsiness as a security from Him, and sends down water on you from the sky to purify you by it, remove from you the defilement of Satan, strengthen your hearts, and make your feet firm by it.﴾

﴿When He covers you with drowsiness as a security from Him﴾ means: He casts sleep upon you as security from Him, the Exalted, (p-2960) after the fear that had afflicted you because of the great number of your enemy.

Fear had kept them awake, so God, exalted is He, cast sleep upon them, and they became secure and rested. God did the same with them on the Day of Uhud, as He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿Then after the distress He sent down upon you security, drowsiness overcoming a group of you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. It is also read as (yughshikum), from al-ighsha' (causing to cover), meaning the act of covering. In both readings the agent is God, exalted is He. It is also read as (yaghshakum), with the verb attributed to the drowsiness (an-nu'as).

In the Sahih it is reported that on the Day of Badr, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in the shelter (al-'arish) with al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), and both of them were supplicating, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was overtaken by a slight sleep. Then he awoke smiling and said: "Rejoice, O Abu Bakr, this is Jibril, dust is on his cheeks (or: on his horses' chests)." Then he went out of the shelter's door reciting: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45].

Then He reminded them of another favour that indicates His victory for them, by His words, glorified is He: ﴿and sends down water on you from the sky to purify you by it﴾, meaning from the minor and major ritual impurity (al-hadath al-asghar wa al-akbar), which is the purification of the outward body. ﴿and removes from you the defilement of Satan﴾, meaning his whisperings, which said: "You are on this sand and cannot fight effectively, and without water what will you do?" God, by sending down that water, removed this, so they had an inward purity. Thus both purities were completed for them, that is, from whisperings or evil thoughts, which is the purification of the inner self. ﴿and strengthens your hearts﴾, meaning He makes them strong with confidence, through security and the removal of fear.

﴿and makes your feet firm by it﴾, meaning on the sand.

Mujahid said: God sent down rain upon them, and by it He settled the dust, the ground became compact, their souls were content, and their feet were made firm.

Al-Jushami said: Al-Qadi said: this is closer to the apparent meaning.

It was also said that it refers to patience and the strength of heart that He poured upon them, until they held firm against their enemy. The pronoun in (bihi, "by it") refers either to the water that was sent down, or to what preceded of the good tidings and victory.

Then God, exalted is He, pointed to a hidden blessing that He manifested to them so that they would thank Him for it, by His words:

(p-2961) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[12] ﴿When your Lord inspired the angels: "I am with you, so make those who believe firm. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve, so strike above the necks and strike every fingertip of them."﴾

﴿When your Lord inspired the angels﴾, i.e., those with whom He reinforced the Muslims, ﴿"I am with you"﴾, i.e., with help and victory.

Al-Jushami said: It may refer to "with the angels" when He sent them as auxiliary support for the Muslims, and it may refer to "with the Muslims," as if it were said: It was inspired to the angels, "I am with the believers, so give them victory and make them firm."

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So make those who believe firm﴾, i.e., by repelling whisperings, and by fighting alongside them and being present as reinforcement and aid. ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., fear.

Then Exalted is He taught them the manner of striking by His saying: ﴿So strike﴾, a command to the believers or to the angels. Accordingly, there is in it evidence that they fought. ﴿Above the necks﴾, i.e., the upper parts of the necks, which are the places of slaughter, so as to send the heads flying, since they are above the necks.

﴿And strike every fingertip of them﴾, i.e., fingers, plural of (banana, a fingertip). It has been said: What is meant by "fingertips" is the extremities in general, figuratively, calling the whole by a part, since they are placed in opposition to the necks and vital spots.

The meaning is: strike them wherever it happens to be, at the vital spots and elsewhere.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[13] ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger. And whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, indeed Allah is severe in penalty.﴾

﴿That﴾ refers to the striking (of necks and fingertips) or to the command to do so. ﴿Because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ means they defied them in what they had legislated.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, indeed Allah is severe in penalty﴾ is a confirmation (taqrir) of what preceded it, if by "the penalty" is meant what befell them in this world; or it is a warning (wa'id) of what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter, after what overtook them in this world, and an explanation of their loss in both abodes.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[14] ﴿That, so taste it; and that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire.﴾

﴿That﴾ is an address to the disbelievers, following the manner of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). ﴿So taste it﴾, i.e., that punishment, O disbelievers, in this world. ﴿And that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire﴾ in the Hereafter.

Then God, exalted is He, forbade fleeing from the battlefield (zahf), clarifying His threat with His words:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[15] ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing (zahf), do not turn your backs to them.﴾

That is, the turning of backs in retreat (al-zuhur bi-l-inhizam). Al-zahf (the advancing mass) is an army that is large; it is named by the verbal noun, and its plural is zuhuf, like fals and fulus.

It is said: zahafa ilayhi, meaning he walked toward it; and zahafa al-sabiyy 'ala istihi, meaning the child crawled on his bottom before he stood up. The walking of a large army to fight was likened to the crawling of children, because by its great number it appears as though it is crawling, that is, moving with a creeping motion before drawing close for striking or spear-thrusting.

Abu al-Su'ud said: ﴿zahfan﴾ is in the accusative, either as a circumstantial state (hal) of the object of ﴿laqitum﴾, meaning advancing toward you, or as a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing an implied verb, which is itself the state, meaning they advance in an advance.

As for it being a state of its subject, or of its object, or of both together, as has been said, this is rejected by His words ﴿so do not turn your backs to them﴾, for there is no sense in restricting the prohibition against turning one's back to their prior advance toward the enemy or to their large number. Rather, the enemy's advance upon them and their large number is what customarily calls for turning one's back and necessitates the prohibition against it.

Interpreting it as an indication of what would happen from them on the day of Hunayn, when they turned their backs in retreat, and they were a zahf of the zuhuf, twelve thousand strong, is far-fetched.

The meaning: when you meet them for fighting, and they are many and numerous while you are few, then do not turn your backs to them, let alone flee. Rather, face them and fight them, let alone bring yourselves close to them in number or equal them.

Al-Shihab said: he deviated from the word "zuhur" (backs) to "adbar" (backs, turned) to make retreat repugnant and to repel from it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 8, verse 16:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[16] ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless he is swerving (mutaharrifan) for battle or joining (mutahayyizan) a company, has indeed earned anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and evil is the destination.﴾

﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ i.e., the day of encounter. ﴿unless he is swerving for battle﴾ i.e., inclining toward it.

It is said: taharrafa, inharafa and ihrawrafa all mean he inclined and deviated. This swerving may be either by turning to fight another group more important than these, or by feigning retreat in order to charge (al-far li al-karr), by making the enemy imagine that he is routed so as to deceive him and draw him out from among his helpers, whereupon he withdraws from him, then charges back upon him alone or together with those of his companions in ambush. This is a category of the stratagems of war. ﴿Or joining a company﴾ i.e., joining another group of Muslims in order to seek their help. ﴿Then he has indeed earned﴾ i.e., returned ﴿anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and evil is the destination﴾ i.e., what he has come to of the torment of the Fire.

Remarks:

The first: The verse indicates the obligation of steadfastness against the enemy, i.e., remaining firm during battle, and the prohibition of fleeing from it on the day of the advancing ranks (yawm al-zahf), and that it is among the major sins, since He threatened severely for it.

The second: The apparent meaning of the verse is general for all believers at all times and in all circumstances, except the case of swerving or joining a company. This is related from Ibn Abbas, and Abu Muslim chose it.

Al-Hakim said: Most of the jurists hold this view.

(p-2964) He also related from a group of the early generation (al-salaf) that the prohibition of the flight mentioned is specific to the day of (Badr), based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾. It is answered that the reference in "on that day" is to the day of the encounter of the advancing ranks, as the context indicates, not to the day of Badr.

The third: A group of the early generation held that the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿or joining a company﴾ is joining another group of Muslims other than the one he is in, whether that group is near or far. It is related that Abu Ubayd was killed on the bridge in the land of Persia, due to the great number of the army from the side of the Magians, and Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: If he had joined me, I would have been a company for him.

In another narration from him: O people! I am your company (fi'atukum).

al-Dahhak said: "The one joining a company" is one who flees to the Prophet and his companions.

Likewise, whoever flees today to his commander or his companions. Ibn Kathir leaned toward this when he said: Whoever flees from a detachment to its commander, or to the supreme Imam, enters into this concession.

Then he cited the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, narrated by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others, who said: "I was in a detachment of the detachments of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the people fled in confusion, and I was among those who fled. We said: How shall we act, for we have fled from the advancing ranks and have earned anger? Then we said: If we entered Medina and spent the night there! Then we said: If we presented ourselves to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then if there is repentance for us, well, and if not, we shall depart! So we came to him before the dawn prayer, and he came out and said: Who are the people? We said: We are the fleeing ones. He said: "No, rather you are the returners (al-'akkarun). I am your company and the company of the Muslims." He said: So we came to him until we kissed his hand."

al-Tirmidhi said: A hasan hadith; we do not know it except from the narration of Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad. End.

That is: and more than one of the imams has spoken about it.

Al-Hakim said in the matter of fleeing: That (p-2965) matter returns to the assessment and effort of the fighter. If he assesses that resistance is possible, fleeing is not lawful; and if he assesses that destruction is certain, fleeing to a company is permitted even if it is far, provided he does not intend to abandon the fronts. The hadith of Ibn Umar mentioned is interpreted accordingly.

It is related from al-Karkhi that steadfastness and perseverance are obligatory when one does not fear annihilation, and knows that he cannot inflict harm upon the unbelievers, and takes refuge in a city of the Muslims or in an army. Thus it is stated absolutely in "Sharh al-Ibanah", so fleeing is not permitted except under these three conditions, and the number mentioned below is not taken into account.

The fourth: It is related from Ata that the ruling of this verse is abrogated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ [al-Anfal: 66]. Al-Hakim said: If reconciliation is possible, there is no abrogation. I say: We have previously pointed out that the early scholars often mean by "naskh" (abrogation) the restriction of the absolute or the specification of the general, so their applying the term "abrogation" to it does not contradict its being muhkam (established).

Some of the imams said: This verse is general, requiring steadfastness even if the number of the polytheists multiplies many times over, but this generality is specified by His words, exalted is He, in this surah: ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand﴾ [al-Anfal: 65].

From Ibn Abbas: Whoever flees from two has fled, and whoever flees from three has not fled.

In sum, there is no contradiction between this verse and the verse of weakness, for this verse is restricted by it, so fleeing from the advancing ranks is forbidden on a condition which Allah has specified in the verse of weakness.

In "al-Muhadhdhab": If their number exceeds twice the number of the Muslims, fleeing is permitted; but if it is predominant in their assessment that they will not be destroyed, steadfastness is preferable; and if they assess destruction, there are two views: withdrawal is obligatory (p-2966) according to His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195].

The second view: it is recommended but not obligatory, because if they are killed they attain martyrdom, and if the number of the unbelievers does not exceed twice the number of the Muslims, then if they do not assess destruction fleeing is not permitted; and if they assess it, there are two views: it is permitted according to His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195], and it is not permitted; and they affirmed the latter in accordance with the apparent meaning of the verse.

Then Almighty Allah explained that their victory on the day of Badr, despite their small number, was by His power and strength, so He, glorified is He, said:

The interpretation of His statement, exalted is He:

[17] ﴿So it was not you who killed them, but Allah killed them. And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw, that He might test the believers with a good trial from Him. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

﴿So you did not kill them﴾, meaning: by your own strength. ﴿But Allah killed them﴾, meaning: He was the cause of their being killed, through your support and their abandonment, He cast terror into their hearts, strengthened your hearts, reinforced you with the angels, and removed from them fear and dismay.

﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾, meaning: you, O Seal of the Prophets, did not throw so that the pebbles reached the faces of the polytheists. ﴿When you threw﴾, meaning: with the pebbles, because a handful of them could not fill the eyes of a large army by a human throw. ﴿But Allah threw﴾, meaning: He delivered them, by causing them to reach the enemy, so as to overpower them.

Abu Muslim said regarding the meaning of the verse: that is, you did not hit when you threw, but Allah hit.

The verb "rama" (to throw/shoot) is only used for hitting the target, and this is evident in their poetry.

It has been narrated from more than one source that the verse was revealed concerning the handful of dust which the Prophet ﷺ flung at the faces of the polytheists on the Day of Badr, when he came out of the shelter (al-'arish), after his supplication, his humble entreaty and his submission. He threw it at them and said: "May the faces be disfigured." Then he commanded his companions to charge immediately after it, and they did so. Allah caused those pebbles to reach the eyes of the polytheists, so none of them remained except that he was struck by what occupied him from his state, and they were routed.

Note:

Al-Jushami said: The verse indicates that the act of the servant is attributed to Him, exalted is He, when it is by His support, help and empowerment, since it is known that they killed and that he threw, and for this reason He said: ﴿when you threw﴾. And for this reason the act of a servant is attributed to the master when his slave carries it out.

It also indicates that the attribution by way of help and command has become stronger, and therefore He said: ﴿So you did not kill them﴾.

In (al-'Inayah) it is said: This verse and the one before it have been cited as evidence that the actions of servants are by the creation of Allah, Exalted, since He negated both killing and throwing.

The meaning is: when you threw, or when you directly handled the operation of the instruments.

The conclusion: "You did not throw creation (i.e., the actual effect) when you threw acquisition (kasb)." Here, kasb (acquisition, the human's appropriation of an act) is the technical term for the Ash'ari doctrine. It was objected that although the claim is true, the verse gives no proof of it, because the apparent contradiction between negation and affirmation is resolved by saying that what is meant is: you did not throw a throw by which you could reach all the eyes, even though you did throw in reality and in form. This is what those mean who say: "You did not throw in reality when you threw in form." So what is negated is the complete throw, and what is affirmed is its basis and a measure of it.

Thus the affirmation and the negation did not apply to one and the same thing, so that one could say: "The negation is in respect of creation, and the affirmation is in respect of direct action." Had this been the intended meaning, the purpose for which the verse was revealed, namely that He affirmed throwing to him because it proceeded from him and negated it from him because its effect is not within human capacity, would not have been established by it. For this reason it was counted as a miracle for him, to the extent that it is as if he had no part in it at all. So the discourse is built on hyperbole, and this does not entail that it fails to correspond to reality, because its literal meaning is not intended. This is how this matter should be understood, for if what was mentioned were the meaning, it would not be specific to this throw, since all the actions of servants are likewise, by their direct performance and by the creation of Allah. End of quotation.

This verification is good, and al-'Allamah Ibn al-Qayyim also drew attention to it in (Zad al-Ma'ad), where he said:

A group has thought that the verse indicates the negation of the act from the servant and its affirmation to Allah, and that He is the actual doer. This is an error on their part for many reasons, which are mentioned elsewhere.

The meaning of the verse is: Allah, glorified is He, affirmed for His Messenger the initiation of the throw, and negated from him the reaching (of the pebbles), which did not occur by his throwing. So "throwing" here refers to the casting and the reaching, and He affirmed for His Prophet the casting, and negated from him the reaching. End of quotation.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that He might test the believers with a good trial from Him﴾, meaning: that He might bestow upon them of His bounty ﴿a good trial﴾, meaning: a beautiful bestowal, through victory, booty and conquest, and then through reward and recompense, without being mixed with the suffering of hardships and adversities, so that they would recognize His right and give thanks to Him.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The lam (of purpose) is either connected to an elided element that comes later, in which case the waw is parenthetical, meaning: and for the sake of benefiting them with victory and booty He did what He did, and not for anything else, which would not benefit them at all. Or it is connected to "threw", in which case the waw is conjunctive, based on an elided cause, meaning: but Allah threw in order to destroy the disbelievers and to test (the believers)... etc. The interpretation of "balaa" (trial) here as bestowal is what the verifiers chose, from their saying: Allah tested him with a trial, a good testing, when He did a beautiful deed for him, and "abla-hu ma'rufan" (He tested him with a kindness). Zuhayr said in his ode which begins with:

Her heart has become sober from Salma, though it almost could not forget, and al-Ta'aniq and al-Thiql have been emptied of Salma.

Al-Ta'aniq and al-Thiql: are places.

May Allah reward with good the two who did for you what they did,
and tested them with the best trial that tests.

That is: (the goodness of their action toward you, so He tested them with the best trial, meaning: Allah did to them the best deed by which He tests His servants, and a human being is tested with good and evil), meaning: He did to them the best deed by which He tests His servants.

Al-Tibi preferred interpreting it as testing in war, based on what follows it. Ibn al-A'rabi said: It is said: "Fulan abla" when he exerted himself in the description of war or generosity, and it is said: "He tested that day a good testing."

﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾, meaning: of their supplication and their appeal for help, ﴿Knowing﴾, meaning: of who deserves victory and triumph.

And His statement, exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[18] ﴿That, and that Allah is weakening the plot of the disbelievers.﴾

﴿That﴾ refers to the good trial (al-bala' al-hasan), or to the killing, or to the throwing. Its place in the sentence is in the nominative case, meaning: the intended matter is, or the matter is, "that."

His saying: ﴿and that Allah is weakening the plot of the disbelievers﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with it, meaning: (p-2969) weakening the might and stratagems of the disbelievers by your victory and their humiliation. That is, the intent is to test the believers and to weaken the plot of the disbelievers.

Ibn Kathir said: This is another good tiding, in addition to the victory that had already occurred, for He informed them that He weakens the plot of the disbelievers in what is yet to come, belittles their affair, and that they are in ruin and destruction. The announced matter was indeed fulfilled according to the announcement, so it became a miracle for the Prophet ﷺ. And to Allah belong praise and grace.

And His saying, Exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[19] ﴿If you seek a decision, then there has certainly come to you the decision. And if you cease, it is better for you. And if you return [to hostility], We will return [to aiding you]. And your company will not avail you anything, although it is numerous. And indeed, Allah is with the believers.﴾

﴿If you seek a decision, then there has certainly come to you the decision﴾ is addressed to the polytheists; that is, if you seek the victory (al-fath), meaning the judgment, and that He should decide between you and your enemies, the believers, then the judgment has come to you with what you asked for.

Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from ʿAbdullah ibn Thaʿlabah that Abu Jahl said, when the two groups met: "O Allah, whichever of us is more severed from kinship and brings what we do not know, destroy him tomorrow morning." So he was the one who sought the decision.

And from al-Suddi: when the polytheists set out from Mecca toward Badr, they took hold of the curtains of the Kaʿbah, sought Allah's help and said: "O Allah, support the mightiest of the two armies, the most noble of the two groups, and the best of the two tribes." Then the Exalted said: ﴿If you seek a decision﴾, the verse.

And from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam: this verse is a report about them of what they said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], the verse. It was said: in this address there is mockery of them, that is, in His words ﴿then there has certainly come to you the decision﴾, because what came to them was destruction and humiliation. Thus [it is reported] in (al-ʿInayah).

This is based on the view that al-fath means victory (al-nasr), but it has another meaning, namely the ruling between two adversaries and judgment (al-qada'). The verse has also been interpreted by both meanings.

﴿And if you cease﴾, that is, from disbelief and hostility toward the Messenger, ﴿it is better for you﴾, that is, in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And if you return﴾, that is, to fighting the Messenger, ﴿We will return﴾, that is, to aiding him against you. ﴿And your company will not avail you anything﴾, that is, will not repel from you anything, ﴿although it is numerous. And indeed, Allah is with the believers﴾, that is, with victory. It was read with the kasra of (inna) as a resumption, and with the fatha of it, on the assumption of the preposition lam.

Note:

It is permissible that the address in His words ﴿If you seek a decision﴾ is to the believers, that is: if you seek victory by your supplication to your Lord, then that has been granted to you, so thank your Lord and adhere to His obedience.

And His words ﴿And if you cease﴾, that is, from disputing concerning the matter of the spoils, and from seeking ransom for the captives, for which you were rebuked by His words ﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that preceded﴾ [al-Anfal: 68], then the Exalted said: ﴿And if you cease﴾ from its like: ﴿it is better for you. And if you return﴾ to those disputes, ﴿We will return against you with rebuke, and the stirring up of the enemy﴾, because the promise of your victory is conditional upon the condition of your continuing in obedience and abandoning opposition. Then the company will not benefit you, nor the number, if Allah is not with you in victory, for He is with those perfect in their faith.

This view was affirmed by al-Razi, who transmitted it from al-Qadi.

al-Baydawi said: The verse following it confirms this, for its intent is the command to obey the Messenger and the prohibition of turning away from him. And Allah knows best.

(p-2971) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[20] ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him⁠﴾ i.e., do not turn away from him by opposing his command. ﴿while you hear⁠﴾ i.e., the Qur'an which speaks of the obligation of obeying him, and the admonitions that restrain from opposing him.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[21] ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾

﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear"﴾ — that is, who claimed hearing. ﴿while they do not hear﴾ — that is, they do not hear with the hearing of reflection and admonition. They are the hypocrites or the polytheists.

What is negated is a particular kind of hearing, yet it is stated in an unrestricted form to indicate that they have been placed in the position of one who has not heard at all, their hearing being treated as though it were non-existent. It has also been said: the hearing here is hearing in the sense of affirming as true (taṣdīq).

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The meaning is that you affirm the Qur'an and prophethood, but when you turn away from obeying the Messenger in some matters, such as the division of the spoils and other things, your affirmation becomes like non-affirmation, and your hearing resembles the hearing of one who does not believe.

Then Allah, exalted is He, clarified the evil state of those who were likened to, as an exaggeration in warning and as an emphasis on the prohibition, by His saying:

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted, interpretation:

[22] ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and dumb who do not reason.﴾

﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures﴾ — i.e., whatever crawls upon the earth, or the worst of beasts. ﴿In the sight of Allah are the deaf﴾ — i.e., deaf to hearing the truth; ﴿the dumb﴾ — i.e., mute in speaking it; ﴿who do not reason﴾ — i.e., do not comprehend it. He, the Exalted, placed them in the category of beasts, because they turned their faculties away from that for which they were created; then He made them the worst of them, because they persisted in obstinacy after understanding, and defied after reason. And in mentioning them in the context of comparison with this expression is the utmost in censure.

The Qur'an has frequently likened the disbelievers to the like of this, such as His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And the example of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and cry﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They are like cattle; rather, they are more astray﴾ [al-A'raf: 179].

The Interpretation of His, the Exalted, Words:

[23] ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were refusing.﴾

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them﴾, meaning: in these deaf and dumb ones, ﴿good﴾, i.e., sincerity and eagerness; ﴿He would have made them hear﴾, meaning: the proofs and admonitions, hearing of comprehension and reflection. That is, He would have made them hearers, so that they would hear as those who affirm. But Allah did not know in them anything of that, since they are wholly empty of it. Therefore He did not make them hear in that manner, since it is devoid of benefit and outside wisdom. To this He alluded by His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away﴾, meaning: if He had made them hear with comprehension, while they were in this state, utterly bare of good, they would have turned away from what they heard of the truth.

﴿while they were refusing﴾, meaning: from accepting it, out of denial and obstinacy.

Al-Razi said: Whatever exists, Allah must know it. So the absence of Allah's knowledge of its existence is a necessary consequence of its non-existence. Therefore it was fitting to express its non-existence in itself by the non-knowledge of Allah of its existence.

Note:

It may be thought that the two conditional clauses in the verse are the premises of a categorical syllogism, thus: "If He knew good in them, He would have made them hear; and if He had made them hear, they would have turned away," which yields: "If He knew good in them, they would have turned away." Its invalidity is clear.

It is answered: this conclusion follows only if the second premise were universal, and that is disallowed.

It was objected that this disallowance, though sound as a matter of logical theory, is an error in interpreting the verse, because it rests on the claim that the stated syllogism lacks the conditions of valid production, and it is not permissible to attribute such a thing to the words of Allah.

It is answered: what is meant is denying that the intent was to construct a syllogism because a condition is absent, not that it is a syllogism that has lost its condition. Just as the non-repetition of the middle term also prevents it. Rather, the purpose of the second premise is to emphasize the first, since its outcome is that hearing was negated because of the absence of good in them; and if hearing had occurred, good would not come about in them, because the locus would not be receptive. So said the author of "al-'Inayah".

Some have attempted to correct its being a conditional syllogism with a unified middle term, valid in production, by positing: "If He knew good in them at some time, they would have turned away after it."

And His, the Exalted, words

The commentary on His saying, Exalted is He:

[24] ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life. And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered.﴾

﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life.﴾ *Al-istijaba* (response) means *al-ijaba* (answering). The poet says:

*"And a caller called, 'O you who answer the call!' But at that moment no responder answered him."*

(He means: no one answered him.) The one who said it is Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi, and the poem is number 14 in *al-Asma'iyyat*.

What is meant by it is obedience and compliance. He used the singular pronoun in His saying ﴿when he calls you﴾, meaning the Messenger, because he is the one who directly carries out the call to Allah, Exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Because his response (ﷺ) is like the response of Allah, Exalted is He, and one of them is mentioned together with the other for emphasis."

As for His saying ﴿that which gives you life﴾, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr said, as related by Ibn Ishaq: that is, for the war through which Allah, Exalted is He, honored you after humiliation, strengthened you after weakness, and protected you from your enemy after they had subdued you.

Jihad was called "life" because in weakening the enemy through it there is life and strength for them, or because it is the cause of martyrdom, which brings about everlasting life, or the cause of the otherworldly reward, which is the source of life. As Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter—that is the [true] life﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 64], meaning the everlasting life. This would then be a *majaz mursal* (a metonymy), by mentioning the cause for the effect, or a metaphor (*isti'ara*). It has also been said that ﴿that which gives you life﴾ means: the religious knowledge which is the basis of the life of the heart, just as ignorance is its death.

Al-Shihab said: The application of "life" to knowledge and "death" to ignorance is a well-known metaphor, mentioned by men of letters and by the scholars of rhetoric (*ahl al-ma'ani*). Al-Zamakhshari recited for someone:

*"Do not be impressed by the ignorant man's fine attire, for he is dead, and his garment is a shroud."*

He also alluded to the saying of Abu al-Tayyib (al-Mutanabbi) from his qasida that begins:

*"The noblest of people are targets for this age; whoever is most free of worry is most free of intelligence."*

And among its lines:

*"Do not be impressed by the beauty of the clothing of one who is wronged, for is the fine quality of the shroud pleasing to one who is buried?"*

The more apparent view is that ﴿that which gives you life﴾ refers to what sets you right of deeds of righteousness and obedience, so that what has preceded and other things are included in it.

**Note:**

The Prophet (ﷺ) used this verse as evidence for the obligation to respond when he calls someone while they are in prayer.

Al-Bukhari related from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: "I was praying when the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by me and called me, but I did not come to him until I had finished my prayer. Then I came to him, and he said: 'What prevented you from coming to me? Did not Allah say: ﴿O you who believe, respond…﴾?'" (the verse).

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart﴾, it admits of several meanings.

First: He, Exalted is He, holds the heart of the man under His control and turns it however He wills. So He intervenes between him and disbelief if He wills to guide him, and between him and faith if He wills to misguide him. This meaning was related by al-Hakim in his *Mustadrak* from Ibn 'Abbas, and he authenticated it, and it was said by more than one of the early scholars (*al-salaf*).

It is supported by what was narrated: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used often to say: 'O Turner of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion.'"

It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, we believe in you and in what you have brought. Do you fear for us?" He said: "Yes, indeed the hearts are between two of the fingers of Allah, Exalted is He; He turns them."

Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi related it from Anas. The wording of Muslim is:

"Indeed the hearts of the children of Adam are between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful, like one heart, He turns it however He wills." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, Turner of the hearts, turn our hearts to Your obedience." Muslim alone, apart from al-Bukhari, related it from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr.

In another narration: "Indeed the heart of the son of Adam is between two of the fingers of Allah; when He wills, He causes it to swerve, and when He wills, He keeps it upright." Ahmad related it from 'A'isha.

Similar has also been narrated from Jabir, Bilal, al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, and Umm Salama, as Ibn Kathir cited.

On this meaning, the verse is a *isti'ara tamthiliyya* (an allegorical metaphor), because of His power over the hearts of the servants, so that He turns them however He wills, in a way that their owner cannot do.

It is likened to one who stands between a person and his property, for he is able to dispose of it while the owner cannot.

Second: He urges haste in obedience before the arrival of death. Thus the meaning of ﴿intervenes between him and his heart﴾ is that He causes him to die, and so the opportunity he has is lost, which is the ability to sincerely purify the heart, to treat its diseases and ailments, and to return it sound as Allah wills. So seize this opportunity and devote it to the obedience of Allah and His Messenger.

Death is thus likened to the interposing between a man and his heart, by which he reasons, in the sense of being unable to know what knowledge would benefit him.

Third: It is a metaphor for the utmost nearness of the servant to Him, because whoever separates two things is closer to each of them than the other is, by being connected to both and the separation of one from the other.

*Yahulu* ("intervenes") is either a *isti'ara taba'iyya* (a derivative metaphor) meaning "brings near," or an *isti'ara tamthiliyya*. This meaning was related from Qatada, who said: "The verse is like His saying: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16]." It contains a warning that He, Exalted is He, is aware of what is hidden in the hearts, of what its owner might be heedless of.

﴿And that to Him you will be gathered﴾, meaning: so that He will recompense you for your deeds.

**On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:**

[25] ﴿And guard against a trial that will not afflict exclusively those among you who have done wrong. And know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

﴿And guard against a trial that will not afflict exclusively those among you who have done wrong.﴾ *Fitnah* (trial, affliction) may mean a sin, such as tolerating what is evil, division of the word (unity), and laziness in jihad. Or it may mean punishment.

If *fitnah* means sin, then its affliction is by the affliction of its effect. If it means punishment, then its affliction is by itself.

The phrase ﴿lā tuṣībanna﴾ (will not afflict) is the answer to the imperative, meaning: the affliction of it does not restrict itself to those among you who directly commit wrongdoing, but it includes them and others through the evil of their companionship and the spread of their vileness to those who mix with them. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum: 41]. This was stated by al-Qashani.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Jarir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no people among whom sins are committed, while they are more powerful and more numerous than those who commit them, and then they do not change it, except that Allah will overspread them with punishment."

Something similar was narrated from Adi ibn Amira, Hudhayfa, al-Nu'man, Aisha and Umm Salama.

(p-2977) Al-Karkhi said: This should not be confused with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir: 18], because when people openly display wrongdoing, it is obligatory upon everyone who sees it to change it, if he is able to do so. If he remains silent, then all of them are sinners: this one does it, and that one is pleased with it. Allah, in His wisdom, has placed the one who is pleased in the same position as the doer, so he is included in the punishment. End of quote.

Al-Qastallani mentioned that the sign of being content with wrongdoing is the absence of pain at the defect that occurs in the religion through the committing of sins. Therefore, a person is not truly shown to be disliking it unless he is pained by the defect that occurs in the religion, just as he is pained and grieved over the loss of his wealth or his child. Thus everyone who is not in this state is content with the wrongdoing, and so the punishment and affliction encompass him on this basis. End of quote.

From Ibn Abbas: Allah commanded the believers not to allow wrongdoing to persist among them, lest Allah overspread them with punishment. ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾, meaning: for those who oppose His commands.

Then the Exalted drew the attention of His servants, the early believers, to His blessings upon them and His kindness toward them, in that they were few and He multiplied them, weak and fearful and He strengthened them and granted them victory, and provided for them from the good things, so that they would thank Him by persisting in obedience. Thus He, glorified is He, said:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[26] ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing that the people would snatch you away, so He sheltered you, strengthened you with His help, and provided you with good things, that perhaps you would be grateful.﴾

﴿And remember﴾, i.e., O company of the Emigrants (muhajirun), ﴿when you were few﴾, i.e., in number, ﴿oppressed in the land﴾, i.e., subdued in the land of Makkah before the Hijrah, Quraysh treating you as weak, ﴿fearing that the people would snatch you away﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah.

And (takhattafahu) and (ikhtatafahu) mean to plunder and take something swiftly. ﴿So He sheltered you﴾, i.e., to Madinah. ﴿And strengthened you with His help﴾, meaning He aided and fortified you on the Day of Badr with His help, through the support of the Ansar, the reinforcement of the angels, and the divine steadfastness. ﴿And provided you with good things﴾, i.e., the spoils of war, since they were not lawful (tayyib) except for you. ﴿That perhaps you would be grateful﴾, i.e., to the Master for what He has favored and bestowed.

That the address in the verse is specifically to the Emigrants, as we have mentioned, is more fitting to the situation and context, and the context indicates it. It has been said that the address is to all the Arabs, and on this is the statement of Qatadah ibn Di'amah al-Sadusi (may Allah have mercy on him) concerning this verse: "This tribe of the Arabs was the most humiliated of people, the most wretched in livelihood, the emptiest in stomachs, the barest in skins, and the most firmly entrenched in misguidance. By Allah, we know of no tribe among the settled peoples of the earth at that time who were in a worse state than them, until Allah brought Islam, through which He established them in the lands, expanded their provision, and made them kings over the necks of the people. And through Islam Allah gave you what you see, so be grateful to Allah for His blessings, for your Lord is a Bestower who loves gratitude, and the people of gratitude are in increase from Allah." End of quotation.

I say: The matter concerning the Arabs, although it is as mentioned, yet applying some of the words of the verse to it involves an evident strain, so the apparent meaning is what we have mentioned.

The commentary on His saying:

[27] ﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger or betray your trusts while you know [it].﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger or betray your trusts while you know [it].﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, reminded them of His bestowing His blessings upon them so that they would be grateful to Him, and gratitude to Him includes standing at His limits, He explained to them what to beware of, which is betrayal.

Included in betraying Allah is neglecting His obligations and transgressing His limits. Included in betraying His Messenger is rejecting his Sunnah and disclosing his secret to the polytheists.
