(p-3046) By "what has been said" he means what al-Razi mentioned in weakening the interpretation of wilayah as inheritance, where he said: Know that the word wilayah does not indicate this meaning, because this word indicates nearness, as we established in several places in this book.

It is said: "the sultan is the walī of whoever has no walī," and this does not signify inheritance. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Verily, the friends of Allah – no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62], and this does not signify inheritance either; rather wilayah signifies nearness, so it can be taken to mean other than inheritance, namely that some of them honour others, are concerned for their affairs, and are specially aided and supported by them. The intent is that they be one hand against the enemies, and that each one's love for the other run in the manner of his love for himself.

When the word admits of this meaning, taking it to mean inheritance is far from the word's indication, especially since they say that this ruling was abrogated by His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿And those related by blood are closer to one another﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. What need compels us to read the word in a sense which the word does not indicate, and then to judge that it was abrogated by another verse mentioned alongside it? This is extremely remote, unless there is a consensus of the exegetes that this is what is meant; then it becomes necessary to turn to it. But the claim of consensus is remote. End.

I say: The generality of this address and its composition has a basis for establishing inheritance, especially since He, the Exalted, negated the allegiance of one who did not emigrate with a negation that encompassed even the closest kin, when He said: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate﴾ – that is, by remaining in their deserts – ﴿you have no obligation of allegiance to them until they emigrate﴾ – that is, to Madinah. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they seek your help in matters of religion, then you must help﴾ – that is, if these Bedouins who did not emigrate seek your help in a religious war, it is obligatory upon you to help them against their polytheist enemies, for they are your brothers in religion – ﴿except against a people between yourselves and whom there is a treaty﴾ – that is, a covenant and a truce for a term – so do not aid them against it, lest you breach your pledge and violate your covenant – ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ – that is, do not oppose His command.

(p-3047) Remarks:

First: Those who held that the intended meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿you have no obligation of allegiance to them﴾ is allegiance in inheritance, and that this is also what is meant in the preceding verse by His saying: ﴿And if they seek your help in matters of religion, then you must help﴾, argued that this is allegiance in religion; therefore the negated allegiance cannot be taken to mean support and backing, since these are required in every case for both parties.

al-Razi answered with what amounts to the following: The wilayah here does not mean absolute taking-as-ally, so as to be refuted by what they mentioned; rather it means a specific sense, namely a strong bond, an emphatic love, a powerful preference, and a firm brotherhood. Support does not necessarily entail allegiance, for a person may support a dhimmi for some reason without taking him as an ally, and may defend his slave or his maid and aid them without taking them as allies – and Allah knows best.

Second: This shows that this verse, like the ones before it, was revealed after the Battle of Badr, and every believer among the desert dwellers was asked to emigrate, so that the number of Muslims would increase and their unity would appear, and so that they would help one another, thereby strengthening their strength through their unity. The request for emigration did not cease until the conquest of Makkah, according to his, the Prophet's (ﷺ), saying: "There is no emigration after the conquest of Makkah." Narrated by al-Bukhari from Mujashi' ibn Mas'ud.

Third: The negation of allegiance from those who did not emigrate at that time included their deprivation of the spoils and the fay'. Imam Ahmad narrated from Buraydah ibn al-Husayb al-Aslami, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (p-3048) appointed a commander over a military expedition, he would enjoin upon him, regarding his own person, the fear of Allah, and goodness toward the Muslims who were with him. He would say: 'Fight in the name of Allah, in the cause of Allah; fight those who disbelieve in Allah. When you meet your enemy from among the polytheists, invite them to three qualities or characteristics; whichever of them they respond to, accept it from them and withhold from them. Invite them to Islam; if they respond, accept from them and withhold from them. Then invite them to move from their land to the land of the emigrants, and inform them that if they do so, they will have what the emigrants have, and upon them will be what is upon the emigrants. If they refuse and choose their own land, inform them that they will be like the Bedouins of the Muslims, the ruling of Allah which applies to the believers will apply to them, and they will have no share in the fay' and the booty, unless they fight alongside the Muslims. If they refuse, invite them to pay the jizyah; if they respond, accept from them and withhold from them. If they refuse, seek help from Allah and fight them.'"

Ibn Kathir said: Muslim alone narrated it, and he has additional narrations.

Fourth: Hamzah read (wilayatihim) with a kasrah on the waw, and the rest read it with a fathah.

al-Shihab said: In the language, wilayah as a verbal noun is attested with fath and with kasr. It was said that they are two dialectal forms with one meaning, namely physical and figurative nearness. It was also said that there is a difference between them: the fath is the wilayah of a client-patron by lineage and the like, and the kasr is the wilayah of the sultan; this was said by Abu ʿUbaydah. It was also said that the fath is from support and lineage, and the kasr is from government; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

al-Asma'i considered the kasr reading to be an error, but he was the one in error, since it is transmitted by mass transmission (mutawatir). The scholars differed in preferring one of the two readings. When the verifying scholars of the language said that fi'alah with kasr in nouns denotes what surrounds a thing and is placed around it like a wrapper or turban, and in verbal nouns occurs in crafts and what is practised through work, such as writing and sewing, al-Zajjaj and those who followed him held that wilayah, because it requires training and practice, was likened to a craft, and therefore it takes the kasr, like imarah (governorship).

This may mean that the coiner, when he coined it, likened it to that, and so it is literal; and it may mean, as in some commentaries on the Kashshaf, that it is a metaphor, just as medicine is called a craft. End.

And His, the Exalted, saying:

(p-3049) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[73] ﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others. If you do not do so, there will be fitnah on earth and great corruption.﴾

﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others﴾ That is, none of them takes as an ally except one of their own. This contains an indication of the prohibition for the Muslims to take them as allies, and of the obligation to keep away from them and cut off relations with them, even if they are close relatives. It has been used as evidence that there is no inheritance between Muslims and disbelievers.

Al-Hakim related in his (Mustadrak) from Usamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The people of two religions do not inherit from one another, and a Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, nor does a disbeliever inherit from a Muslim," then he recited: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ — the verse. It was related by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from him with the wording: "A Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, nor does a disbeliever inherit from a Muslim."

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you do not do so, there will be fitnah on earth and great corruption﴾ That is: if you do not do what I have commanded you of maintaining ties and supporting one another, and of severing the bonds between you and the disbelievers, there will occur fitnah on earth and a great mischief. For as long as the Muslims do not become one hand against polytheism, the condition is evident and the corruption is increased, in beliefs and in deeds.

It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿do﴾ refers to the covenant, or to its safeguarding, or to victory, or to affirmation. And it has been said that it refers to the seeking of help (istinsar) understood from the verb, and the fitnah is the neglect of the believers who seek help from us, until the disbelievers gain power over us, since this entails weakness for the religion. ?

Al-Shihab said: In this there is strain; that is, the more apparent view is that it refers to the taking of allies and the maintaining of ties, as we have explained.

Al-Razi said: The explanation of this fitnah and corruption has several aspects:

The first: If the Muslims mixed with the disbelievers at a time when the Muslims were weak and few in number and the disbelievers were strong and many, that mixing would perhaps become a cause for the Muslim to join the disbelievers.

(p-3050) The second: If the Muslims were scattered, a large body would not appear from them, and that would become a cause for the disbelievers' boldness against them.

The third: If all the Muslims increase every day in number and equipment, that would become a cause for greater eagerness among them for what they are engaged in, and for the eagerness of the dissenter to join them. End.

And His saying, Exalted is He:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[74] ﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the way of Allah, and those who gave shelter and helped—those are the believers in truth. For them is forgiveness and a noble provision.﴾

﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the way of Allah, and those who gave shelter and helped—those are the believers in truth. For them is forgiveness and a noble provision.﴾ This is a return to the mention of the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar), for praise of them and testimony to them, together with the noble promise. There is no repetition, since the context of the first (verse) is to make mutual solidarity (tawasul) among them obligatory, whereas their mention here is to show the magnitude of their station and the loftiness of their rank.

Al-Razi said: Its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: that the repetition indicates greater concern for their condition, and that indicates nobility and exaltation.

The second: that He, exalted is He, praised them here in three ways:

The first of them: His saying, ﴿those are the believers in truth﴾. His saying, ﴿those are the believers﴾, conveys restriction (hasr), and His saying, ﴿in truth﴾, conveys emphasis in describing them as being truthful and genuinely committed on the path of religion. And they were indeed so, for whoever is not truthful in his religion would not have borne abandoning the former religions, would not have left family and homeland, would not have expended self and wealth, and would not have been among those who hasten and compete in these circumstances.

The second of them: His saying, ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, where the indefinite form indicates completeness, i.e., perfect, complete forgiveness.

The third of them: His saying, ﴿and a noble provision﴾, where what is meant is the lofty, honourable reward. End of quotation.

(p-3051) Allah, exalted is He, has praised the Emigrants and the Helpers in more than one verse of His Noble Book—and Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 8, verse 75 (part 1 of 2)**

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[75] ﴿And those who believed afterwards and emigrated and strove alongside you, they are of you. And blood relatives are nearer to one another in the Book of God. Indeed, God is Knowing of all things.﴾

﴿And those who believed afterwards and emigrated and strove alongside you, they are of you﴾: that is, they are of your number, namely the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the Helpers (al-Ansar), in deserving what you have deserved of loyalty and support, the perfection of faith, forgiveness, and generous provision.

Is the meaning of His words "afterwards" (min ba'du) to be taken as after the first emigration, or after al-Hudaybiyya, which was the second emigration, or after the revelation of this verse, or after the Battle of Badr? I say: the noble wording encompasses all of these, and restricting it to one of them is a restriction without a restricting proof.

﴿And blood relatives are nearer to one another in the Book of God﴾: that is, in His decree and His allotment, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh), or in the Qur'an, since the Book of God is applied to each of these. ﴿Indeed, God is Knowing of all things﴾, so He judges among His servants by whatever rulings He wills, which are the ultimate in correctness, wisdom and goodness.

**Notes (tanbihat):**

**The first:** This verse abrogates (naskh, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one) the inheritance arising from loyalty and support, according to those who interpret His earlier saying, ﴿some of them are nearer to some﴾, and what follows it, as referring to inheritance.

Abu Dawud related from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A man used to form an alliance with another man, with no kinship between them, and one of them would inherit from the other. Then the verse of al-Anfal abrogated that, when He said: ﴿And blood relatives...﴾ and so on." However, in its chain of narration there is someone who has been criticised (maqal).

As for those who interpret the loyalty mentioned earlier as support, aid and honour, they take this verse as a report from Him, glorified and exalted is He, that relatives are nearer to one another. That is because the earlier verse, since it was open to the reading of inheritance-based guardianship, God Exalted explained in this verse that the guardianship of inheritance arises only through kinship, except what the evidence specifies. So the purpose of the verse is to remove this misunderstanding.

Al-Razi said: "This is preferable, because multiplying abrogation without necessity or need is not permissible."

**The second:** Those who make dhawu al-arham (kin who are neither agnatic heirs nor Qur'anically fixed sharers) heirs have cited this verse. They are those who are neither 'asaba (agnates, residuary heirs) nor dhawu al-sihaam (those with fixed shares). He said: "It is supported by the hadith: 'The maternal uncle is the heir of the one who has no heir.'" Those who deny their inheritance have answered that the verse's meaning concerns those mentioned by God among the fixed-share holders and the agnates, and the hadith means: "Whoever has his heir as a maternal uncle, has no other heir." It was rebutted that the verse is general, so there is no reason to restrict it, and that the meaning of the hadith is: "Whoever has no heir other than him," in accordance with the hadith: "I am the pillar of the one who has no pillar."

Then, those who established their inheritance differed over whether they inherit by proximity (al-qurb) or by substitution (al-tanzil), whether the nearer relative takes precedence over the more distant, and whether the male is preferred over the female. The verse is open to these possibilities. This was reported by some of the Zaydi exegetes.

Ibn Kathir said: "The meaning of His saying ﴿blood relatives﴾ is not the specific category that the scholars of the laws of inheritance (ilm al-fara'id) apply to relatives who have neither a fixed share nor agnatic status. Rather, they are linked through an heir, such as the maternal aunt and uncle, the paternal aunt, the children of daughters, the children of sisters, and the like, as some claim, who argue from the verse and firmly believe this on the question. Rather, the truth is that the verse is general, encompassing all kinship relations, as explicitly stated by Ibn 'Abbas [p. 3053], Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Hasan, Qatada and others. On this basis it includes dhawu al-arham by this specific name, and those who do not grant them inheritance argue from other proofs, the strongest of which is the hadith: 'God has given every person with a right his right, so there is no bequest to an heir.'"

They said: "If he had a right, he would have a named share in the Book of God. Since he does not, he is not an heir." End of quote.

The weakness of this argument is not hidden, for the establishment of a right does not necessitate the specification of a fixed share. Moreover, the meaning of the hadith is: "He has given each person with a right his right, in detail and in summary," and He has given them the general right of priority, and entrusted to those firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rasikhun) the explanation of what is understood from the general inheritance, by its generality, through deduction and understanding, according to the rule of the general statements of revelation.

I have seen in this question an admirable discussion which al-Hasan al-Sabi included in the *Tarikh al-Wuzara'* (History of the Viziers), in the reports about the vizierate of Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Furat. We transmit it here because it is comprehensive and complete. He, may God have mercy on him, said:

The text of what Abu Khazim wrote to Badr al-Mu'tadidi, in reply to a letter addressed to him concerning the matter of inheritances, was: The letter of the Amir arrived, mentioning that he needed my view on what I consider obligatory from the inheritance money for the public treasury (bayt al-mal), and the money that I consider obligatory from it. The summary and explanation of that, and I mention to the Amir what has come to me of the answer on this question and the proof concerning what he asked, so that he may understand it, God willing:

People differ regarding the inheritance of relatives. It is reported from Zayd ibn Thabit that he assigned the estate, when the deceased has no heir from among the agnates or fixed-share holders, to the community of Muslims and their treasury. He also said the same regarding the remainder after the stated shares, if there are no agnates. No one among the Companions is reported to have said this except Zayd ibn Thabit.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud disagreed with him, and they made the surplus of the shares a return (radd) to the fixed-share holders from among the relatives, and they made the property belong to the blood relative when there is no other heir.

The Sunna supports what was reported from them and contradicts what was reported from Zayd ibn Thabit. The interpretation of the Qur'an requires what they held. No one may say, contrary to the Sunna and the revelation, by personal opinion (ra'y).

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And blood relatives are nearer to one another in the Book of God, indeed God is Knowing of all things﴾. So He made the nearer relative preferable to the more distant. This is the view that 'Umar, 'Ali and 'Abd Allah, may God be pleased with them, took, and those Imams who followed them adopted it, relied upon it, and held fast to it. And God knows best.

If there were in this question something indicated by a witness from the Book and the Sunna, then it would be obligatory to follow the most excellent and most numerous of the earliest predecessors, and to abandon accepting anyone else who does not reach their rank in precedence.

If the matter of the people is returned to choice among the statements of the early generation, is it conceivable to anyone that Zayd's knowledge does not equal the knowledge of 'Umar, 'Ali and 'Abd Allah? And if they are preferred in precedence and emigration, from where did it become obligatory to follow what was reported from Zayd ibn Thabit and to discard what was reported from them, when they also cited the Book for what they held, and the Sunna for what they ruled?

The report from the Prophet ﷺ is established regarding the inheritance of those relatives who have no fixed share in the Book. Among that is what was related to us from Mu'awiya ibn Salih, from Rashid ibn Sa'd, from Abu 'Amir al-Harawi, from al-Miqdam ibn Ma'd Yakrib, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "The maternal uncle is the heir of the one who has no heir; he inherits his property and pays his blood-money (ya'qilu 'anhu)."

Likewise it reached us from Sharik ibn 'Abd Allah, from Layth, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, the like of it. And from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Umar ibn Salama, from Tawus, from 'A'isha, that the Prophet ﷺ said the like of that.

It is mentioned from 'Ubada ibn Abi 'Abbad, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Ya'qub ibn 'Utba, from Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Habban, from his paternal uncle Wasi' ibn Habban, who said: "Thabit ibn Abi al-Dahdah died, and the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Asim ibn 'Adi: 'Does he have a kinsman among you?'" [p. 3054]

He said: "So he gave his estate to the son of his sister, and so he (peace be upon him) made it obligatory." Through what this report transmits, it is established that inheritance goes to one who has no share among relatives, in the absence of those with the shares specified in the Book.

He also gave the grandmother a sixth of the inheritance, though she has no fixed share, and there is agreement on this. In what he assigned to her of a sixth, there is evidence that whoever has no share among relatives is of the same status, when the shares are void and he is not of their number, and that he has a better claim to inheritance than the stranger.

What is reported from Zayd ibn Thabit is that he assigned the surplus over the fixed shares, and the entire estate when the shares are exhausted after their holders, to the community of Muslims, making them all heirs. And what reaches them of that, in contrast to the property of the fay' (booty without fighting) disbursed to the garrison, the soldiers' stipends, and the public interests, when that is the case, would be what is reported from him to all people. Their number cannot be counted, and it is impossible to divide it among them while they are scattered across the far corners of the earth, east and west.

When that is impossible and leads to what is not possible, it is refuted, and what we have said, from the words of the greatest Imams, is established.

Some interpreters have construed the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿And blood relatives are nearer to one another in the Book﴾, and said regarding it: People used to inherit by alliance (hilf) rather than kinship. When God made the inheritances due to their people among the relatives, He prevented the ally by what He prescribed of shares. They erred and turned the ruling of the verse to specificity. That is not obligatory in the absence of evidence, because its form in revelation is the form of generality.

Furthermore, if its interpretation were what they claimed, and the shares that were abrogated were what the ally would inherit before the revelation of the obligatory shares, then it would have been required from the beginning, and what they said would mean that if the deceased has no heir among the fixed-share holders, the two allies would inherit in accordance with their first obligation and the earlier ruling. For what prevented them, if this interpretation is established, is "one who has a share" rather than "one who has no share." So when the preventer is removed, the ruling returns to its beginning.

There is no disagreement between the two groups that the ally does not inherit from the ally today, even if he has no other heir. This indicates the corruption of their interpretation, and that what is meant in the verse which made the right due to relatives is other than what they claimed, for God, glorified is He, only intended by its meaning that the nearer relative is specifically entitled to inheritance rather than the more distant.

It may be necessary for whoever adopts the report from Zayd while abandoning the report from 'Umar, 'Ali and 'Abd Allah, peace be upon them, to drop the mutual liability (ta'aqul) between the stranger and the relative, and to make the blood relative preferable, since he does not prefer the stranger by kinship.

The arrangement of inheritances in principle follows the precedence of one over another in closeness of relation, such as the full brother, the consanguine brother, the full paternal cousin, and the consanguine paternal cousin. Their specificity to the nearer relative in inheritance when all are combined is decisive. God the Exalted said: ﴿God instructs you concerning your children: for the male, the equal of the share of two females﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. The children's children, whether further down or further up, are all covered by this designation. However, the nearer among them is, in the sense of the verse, more entitled than the more distant. If that is so, then the nearer relative is preferable to the stranger in the estate, by the kinship through which he draws near, to the exclusion of the other.

Furthermore, the scholars are a small group who do not know the correct view on this question, except what is reported from the two Caliphs 'Umar and 'Ali, may God's blessings be upon them both, and what is reported from Ibn Mas'ud. Then they did not restrict their emphasis and proof for the inheritance of the blood relative except to what is reported from 'Abd Allah ibn al-'Abbas, grandfather of the Commander of the Faithful, may God prolong his life, interpreter of the Qur'an, sea of knowledge, one whom people fell silent to hear when he spoke, and for whom the Prophet ﷺ prayed, saying: "O God, grant him understanding in religion and teach him the interpretation." The prayer of the Prophet ﷺ is answered. And whoever knows the interpretation of the Qur'an best, following him in it is most obligatory.

وقَدْ رُوِيَ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ مِن قَوْلِ عُمَرَ وعَلِيٍّ (p-٣٠٥٧) وعَبْدِ اللَّهِ والجَماعَةِ، وما زالَتِ الخُلَفاءُ مِن أجْدادِ أمِيرِ المُؤْمِنِينَ، أعَزَّهُ اللَّهُ، يَسْتَقْضُونَ الحُكّامَ، فَيَقْضُونَ بِرَدِّ المَوارِيثِ عَلى الأقارِبِ، ولا يُنْكِرُونَ ذَلِكَ عَلى مَن قَضى بِهِ مِن قُضاتِهِمْ، ولا تَرُدُّونَهُ مُتَجاوِزًا لِلْحَقِّ فِيهِ، وما عُرِفَتِ الجَماعَةُ بِغَيْرِ هَذا الِاسْمِ إلّا مُنْذُ نَحْوِ عِشْرِينَ سَنَةً، وأمِيرُ المُؤْمِنِينَ أوْلى مَنِ اتَّبَعَ آثارَ السَّلَفِ، واقْتَدى بِخُلَفاءِ اللَّهِ، ومالَ إلى أفْضَلِ المَذْهَبَيْنِ، وإلى اللَّهِ الرَّغْبَةُ في عِصْمَةِ الأمِيرِ، وتَسْدِيدِهِ، والحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ. انْتَهى. (End of quote.)

ونَقَلَ أبُو الحَسَنِ الصّابِيُّ قَبْلَ نُسْخَةٍ أبِي الحَسَنِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ جَعْفَرِ بْنِ ثَوابَةَ في المَوارِيثِ، وفِيها نَقْلُ ما كَتَبَهُ عَبْدُ الحَمِيدِ في كِتابِ مَوارِيثِ أهْلِ المِلَّةِ، وأنَّهُ حَكى فِيهِ أنَّ عُمَرَ بْنَ الخَطّابِ وعَلِيَّ بْنَ أبِي طالِبٍ وعَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ عَبّاسٍ، وعَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ مَسْعُودٍ رِضْوانُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِمْ ومَنِ اتَّبَعَهم مِنَ الأئِمَّةِ الهادِينَ رَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِمْ، رَأوْا أنْ يُرَدَّ عَلى أصْحابِ السِّهامِ (the Qur'anically fixed sharers, i.e., heirs with prescribed shares) مِنَ القَرابَةِ ما يَفْضُلُ عَنِ السِّهامِ المُفْتَرَضَةِ في كِتابِ اللَّهِ تَبارَكَ وتَعالى مِنَ المَوارِيثِ، وإذا لَمْ يَكُنْ لِلْمُتَوَفّى عَصَبَةٌ (agnatic heirs, male relatives who inherit the residue) يَحُوزُ باقِيَ مِيراثِهِ، وجَعَلُوا رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهم تَرِكَةَ مَن يُتَوَفّى ولا عَصَبَةَ لَهُ لِذَوِي رَحِمَهُ، إنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ وارِثٌ سِواهم، مُمْتَثِلِينَ في ذَلِكَ أمْرَ اللَّهِ سُبْحانَهُ إذْ يَقُولُ: ﴿وأُولُو الأرْحامِ بَعْضُهم أوْلى بِبَعْضٍ في كِتابِ اللَّهِ إنَّ اللَّهَ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ﴾ وسُنَّةُ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ (ﷺ) في تَوْرِيثِهِ مَن لا فَرْضَ لَهُ في كِتابِ اللَّهِ تَعالى مِنَ الخالِ وابْنِ الأُخْتِ والجَدَّةِ. انْتَهى.

الثّالِثُ: اسْتَدَلَّ بِالآيَةِ الإمامِيَّةُ (the Imamiyya, the Twelver Shi'a) عَلى تَقْدِيمِ الإمامِ عَلِيٍّ كَرَّمَ اللَّهُ وجْهَهُ عَلى غَيْرِهِ في الإمامَةِ، لِانْدِراجِها في عُمُومِ الأوْلَوِيَّةِ.

والجَوابُ - عَلى فَرْضِ صِحَّةِ هَذِهِ الدَّلالَةِ - أنَّ العَبّاسَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ كانَ أوْلى بِالإمامَةِ، لِأنَّهُ كانَ أقْرَبَ إلى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ (ﷺ) مِن عَلِيٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.
